newsitem.title: USA: ASARCO expects copper deficit in 1997/1998.
newsitem.headline: ASARCO expects copper deficit in 1997/1998.

text.p: ASARCO, the U.S. base metals group, said the copper market is set to remain in a deficit this year and next as strong consumption eats up new supplies.

ASARCO chairman, president and chief executive officer Richard de J Osborne said total stocks of copper will stay low at just 3.3 weeks' of consumption at the end of 1997 and 2.6 weeks at the end of next year.

The Western world's copper market will be in deficit to the tune of 17,000 tonnes of refined metal this year and 143,000 tonnes in 1998, Osborne said in a lunchtime presentation to the American Metal Market's copper seminar.
"The Western world has been in a continued supply deficit for the last three years. Since 1993 Western world consumption has absorbed all of that supply," Osborne said.
ASARCO, which has a majority stake in Southern Peru Copper Co, claims to be the world's fourth biggest non-state owned copper producer.

Osborne's forecasts fly in the face of the bulk of metals industry analysts who expect a growing surplus of copper hitting the markets from this year onwards as Latin America in particular cranks up red metal output.
Osborne dismissed talk of large hidden stockpiles of metal, rumors of which caused prices to wobble last year.
Western world copper consumption was set to grow 3 percent this year and a further 3.6 percent in 1998 compared to 3.2 percent in 1996.
The Western world will need 1.1 million tonnes of extra copper over the next two years above last year's total, Osborne forecast.
Growth in copper demand in Western Europe this year was expected to be about one percent, rising to 2.8 percent in 1998. Growth in Japan would be modest, but stronger elsewhere in Asia.

But the continuing, albeit to a lesser degree, smelter bottleneck may prove to be a problem. Osborne said ASARCO recently decided to keep its Ray mine on an extended shutdown until September this year because it lacked smelter capacity to handle the concentrates.
